title: TN Visa Estimated Tax Payments: Avoid $5,000+ Penalties on Stock Income
description: Complete 2026 guide to quarterly estimated tax payments for TN visa workers with RSUs and stock options. Learn safe harbor rules, Form 1040-ES, and strategies to avoid underpayment penalties.
content:
## Key Takeaways

- TN visa workers with stock compensation typically **owe $8,000-25,000** in quarterly estimated taxes
- **Underpayment penalty:** 8% annual interest on the shortfall ($800-2,500 for most workers)
- **Safe harbor:** Pay 100-110% of prior year tax to avoid penalties (even if you underpay current year)
- Most TN workers **don't make estimated payments** and get hit with penalties
- Free calculator below shows exact quarterly payment amounts

## Why TN Visa Workers Owe Estimated Taxes

### Your Employer Doesn't Withhold Enough

When your RSUs vest or stock options are exercised, your employer withholds taxes at a **flat 22% federal rate** (or 37% if vesting > $1M/year).

But your actual tax liability might be **32-37%** depending on your total income.

**Example: Meta L5 Engineer**

```
Salary: $180,000
RSU vesting (2026): $200,000
Total income: $380,000

Automatic withholding:
Salary (24% average): $43,200
RSU (22% flat): $44,000
Total withheld: $87,200

Actual tax owed:
Federal (effective 30%): $114,000
California (effective 11%): $41,800
Total owed: $155,800

Shortfall: $155,800 - $87,200 = $68,600
```

You're **underwithheld by $68,600**.

If you don't make quarterly estimated payments, the IRS charges you **8% annual interest** on $68,600.

**Penalty:** $5,488 for one year

That's $5,488 you threw away by not paying quarterly.

### The IRS Expects Quarterly Payments

The US tax system is **pay-as-you-go**. The IRS expects you to pay tax throughout the year, not all at once on April 15.

**If you owe $1,000+ at tax time**, you're subject to underpayment penalties.

**Exception:** You won't owe penalties if you meet **safe harbor rules** (explained below).

---

## Who Must Make Estimated Tax Payments?

### The $1,000 Test

You must make estimated payments if:

1. You expect to owe **$1,000 or more** when you file your return, AND
2. Your withholding will be **less than** the smaller of:
   - **90%** of current year tax, OR
   - **100%** of prior year tax (110% if prior year AGI > $150,000)

**Example 1: TN Worker Needs Estimated Payments**

```
2025 tax liability: $40,000
2026 expected tax: $80,000 (big RSU vesting)
2026 withholding: $50,000

Test:
Expected amount owed: $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000 (> $1,000) ✅

Withholding vs safe harbor:
90% of 2026 tax: $72,000
100% of 2025 tax: $40,000 (lower)

Withholding: $50,000 > $40,000 safe harbor ✅

Result: NO estimated payments required (safe harbor met)
```

Even though you'll owe $30,000, you're protected by safe harbor.

**Example 2: TN Worker Must Pay Estimated**

```
2025 tax liability: $20,000 (first year, low income)
2026 expected tax: $80,000 (big RSU vesting)
2026 withholding: $50,000

Test:
Expected amount owed: $30,000 (> $1,000) ✅

Withholding vs safe harbor:
90% of 2026 tax: $72,000
100% of 2025 tax: $20,000 (lower)

Withholding: $50,000 < $72,000 (90% threshold) ❌

Result: MUST make estimated payments for $22,000 ($72K - $50K)
```

You don't meet safe harbor. You must make quarterly payments.

---

## Safe Harbor Rules Explained

### Three Ways to Avoid Penalties

You're safe from underpayment penalties if you meet **any** of these:

**Safe Harbor 1: Prior Year Tax**
Pay at least **100%** of last year's total tax (110% if last year AGI > $150,000).

**Safe Harbor 2: Current Year Tax**
Pay at least **90%** of this year's total tax.

**Safe Harbor 3: Small Balance**
You owe **less than $1,000** when you file.

### Which Safe Harbor to Use?

**Use Prior Year (Safe Harbor 1) if:**
- Your income is **increasing** this year (big RSU vesting, promotion, bonus)
- You want **predictability** (you know last year's tax amount)
- You don't want to estimate current year income

**Use Current Year (Safe Harbor 2) if:**
- Your income is **decreasing** this year (changed jobs, smaller vesting)
- You want to **pay less** upfront (90% vs 100-110%)

**Example: Prior Year Safe Harbor**

```
2025 total tax: $50,000
2026 expected tax: $100,000 (big jump)

Safe harbor target:
100% of 2025 tax = $50,000

Withholding in 2026: $60,000

Result: $60,000 > $50,000 safe harbor ✅

No estimated payments needed!

At tax time, you'll owe $40,000 ($100K - $60K), but no penalties.
```

This is the **"increase your W-4 withholding"** strategy.

---

## Quarterly Payment Deadlines

### 2026 Estimated Tax Due Dates

| Quarter | Income Period | Due Date |
|---------|---------------|----------|
| Q1 | Jan 1 - Mar 31 | April 15, 2026 |
| Q2 | Apr 1 - May 31 | June 16, 2026 |
| Q3 | Jun 1 - Aug 31 | September 15, 2026 |
| Q4 | Sep 1 - Dec 31 | January 15, 2027 |

**Important notes:**
- Q2 is only **2 months** (not 3)
- Q3 is **3 months**
- Q4 is **4 months**

**Penalty calculation:** If you miss a deadline, the IRS charges interest from the due date until you pay.

### Alternative: Pay by January 31

You can **skip Q4 payment** (Jan 15) if you file your tax return and pay in full by **January 31**.

**Example:**

Instead of:
- Q4 payment: $20,000 due Jan 15, 2027
- File tax return: April 15, 2027

You can:
- File tax return: January 31, 2027
- Pay full balance: $20,000 with return

**Benefit:** Avoid Q4 payment, no penalty

**Catch:** You need to file 2.5 months early (most people don't have W-2s yet)

---

## How to Calculate Estimated Payments

### Method 1: Annualized Income (Precise)

Calculate tax liability **quarter by quarter** based on actual income received.

Use **Form 2210 Schedule AI** (Annualized Income Installment Method).

**Example: Meta RSU Vesting in Q3**

```
Q1 income: $45,000 (salary only)
Q2 income: $45,000 (salary only)
Q3 income: $45,000 salary + $200,000 RSU = $245,000
Q4 income: $45,000 (salary only)

Quarterly payments (annualized method):
Q1: $4,000 (on $45K × 4 = $180K annualized)
Q2: $4,000 (same)
Q3: $65,000 (big jump for RSU)
Q4: $4,000 (back to normal)

Total: $77,000
```

You pay **when you receive the income**, not evenly throughout the year.

**Pros:**
- Most accurate
- No overpayment (don't give IRS a free loan)

**Cons:**
- Complex calculation (need Form 2210 Schedule AI)
- Must track income quarterly

### Method 2: Equal Quarterly Payments (Simple)

Divide total expected tax by 4, pay evenly.

**Example:**

```
Expected 2026 tax: $100,000
Withholding: $60,000
Shortfall: $40,000

Quarterly payments:
Q1: $10,000 (April 15)
Q2: $10,000 (June 16)
Q3: $10,000 (Sept 15)
Q4: $10,000 (Jan 15)

Total: $40,000
```

**Pros:**
- Simple (divide by 4)
- Predictable

**Cons:**
- You might overpay early (if income is back-loaded)
- Tie up cash unnecessarily

### Method 3: Safe Harbor (Prior Year)

Pay 100-110% of prior year tax, split evenly.

**Example:**

```
2025 total tax: $50,000
2026 safe harbor: 100% × $50,000 = $50,000
2026 withholding: $30,000
Additional needed: $20,000

Quarterly payments:
Q1-Q4: $5,000 each

Total: $20,000
```

**Pros:**
- Guaranteed no penalties (even if you underestimate 2026 tax)
- Simple (use last year's tax return)

**Cons:**
- Might overpay (if 2026 income is lower)
- Doesn't account for income changes

## TN Visa Worker Example: Real Calculation

**Profile:**
- Salary: $160,000 (Shopify, remote to Canada)
- RSU vesting in 2026: $150,000 (August)
- Stock option exercise: $50,000 (November)
- State: California (high tax)

### Step 1: Estimate 2026 Tax

**Federal:**
```
Gross income: $160K + $150K + $50K = $360,000
Standard deduction: -$14,600
Taxable income: $345,400

Tax calculation:
$0-$11,600: 10% = $1,160
$11,600-$47,150: 12% = $4,266
$47,150-$100,525: 22% = $11,743
$100,525-$191,950: 24% = $21,942
$191,950-$243,725: 32% = $16,568
$243,725-$345,400: 35% = $35,586

Total federal: $91,265
```

**California:**
```
CA taxable income: $360,000
CA tax (13.3% top bracket, ~10.5% effective): $37,800
```

**Total tax:** $91,265 + $37,800 = **$129,065**

### Step 2: Calculate Withholding

**Salary withholding:**
```
Federal: $160,000 × 22% average = $35,200
CA: $160,000 × 9% average = $14,400
```

**RSU withholding (August):**
```
Federal: $150,000 × 22% = $33,000
CA: $150,000 × 13.3% = $19,950
```

**Stock option withholding (November):**
```
Federal: $50,000 × 37% = $18,500
CA: $50,000 × 13.3% = $6,650
```

**Total withholding:** $127,700

### Step 3: Determine Estimated Payment Requirement

```
Expected tax: $129,065
Withholding: $127,700
Shortfall: $1,365
```

**Test:**
- Owe > $1,000? Yes ($1,365) ✅
- Need estimated payments? Check safe harbor:

**Assume 2025 tax was $60,000:**
```
Safe harbor (100% of prior): $60,000
Withholding: $127,700 > $60,000 ✅

Result: NO estimated payments needed (safe harbor met)
```

Even though they owe $1,365 at tax time, they're protected by prior year safe harbor.

**No penalty.**

### Step 4: If Safe Harbor Wasn't Met

Assume 2025 tax was only $10,000 (first year):

```
Safe harbor (100% of prior): $10,000 (too low)
90% of current: 90% × $129,065 = $116,159

Withholding: $127,700 > $116,159 ✅

Result: STILL no estimated payments needed (90% safe harbor met)
```

Withholding is high enough to cover 90% of current year tax.

**No penalty.**

### Penalty Scenario: What If Withholding Was Lower?

Assume withholding was only $80,000:

```
Expected tax: $129,065
Withholding: $80,000
Shortfall: $49,065

Safe harbor check:
90% of current: $116,159
Withholding: $80,000 < $116,159 ❌

Must pay estimated: $116,159 - $80,000 = $36,159
```

They need to make **$36,159 in estimated payments** across Q1-Q4.

If they don't, they owe **underpayment penalty**:

**Penalty calculation:**
```
Underpayment: $36,159
Penalty rate: 8% annual (2026 rate)
Average underpayment period: 6 months

Penalty: $36,159 × 8% × 0.5 = $1,446
```

They owe **$1,446 in penalties** for not making estimated payments.

## Strategies to Avoid Estimated Payments

### Strategy 1: Increase W-4 Withholding

Instead of making quarterly payments, increase your paycheck withholding.

**How:**
File new **Form W-4** with your employer:
- Line 4(c): Extra withholding

**Example:**
```
You need $40,000 additional withholding for the year.
Paychecks: 26 (bi-weekly)

Extra withholding per paycheck: $40,000 / 26 = $1,538

File W-4:
Line 4(c): $1,538
```

Your employer withholds an extra $1,538 per paycheck.

**Pros:**
- ✅ Automatic (no quarterly deadlines)
- ✅ Spreads burden over whole year
- ✅ No risk of missing payments

**Cons:**
- ❌ Reduces take-home pay
- ❌ Not optimal if income is lumpy (big Q3 vesting)

### Strategy 2: One-Time Withholding Request

Some employers allow you to request **extra withholding on RSU vesting**.

**How:**
Contact your equity administrator (Shareworks, E*TRADE, Equity Edge) before vesting:

> "I want to withhold 40% federal + 15% state on my upcoming RSU vesting (instead of standard 22% + 13.3%)."

**Example:**
```
RSU vesting: $200,000
Standard withholding: 35.3% = $70,600
Requested withholding: 55% = $110,000

Extra withheld: $39,400
```

This extra withholding counts toward your annual tax liability.

**Pros:**
- ✅ Withheld when you receive the income (perfect timing)
- ✅ No quarterly payments

**Cons:**
- ❌ Not all employers allow this
- ❌ Reduces net proceeds from vesting

### Strategy 3: Annualized Income Method

If your income is **heavily back-loaded** (big Q4 vesting), use the annualized income method to pay **only when you receive income**.

**Example:**

Income:
- Q1-Q3: $45,000/quarter (salary only)
- Q4: $45,000 + $300,000 RSU = $345,000

**Standard quarterly payments:**
```
Total tax: $150,000
Withholding: $60,000
Estimated needed: $90,000

Q1-Q4: $22,500 each
```

You pay $67,500 in Q1-Q3 (before you receive the RSU).

**Annualized income method:**
```
Q1: $3,000 (on $45K × 4 = $180K annualized income)
Q2: $3,000
Q3: $3,000
Q4: $81,000 (on actual $435K total income)

Total: $90,000 (same total, but paid when income is received)
```

You only pay $9,000 in Q1-Q3, then $81,000 in Q4 (after RSU vests).

**Pros:**
- ✅ Optimize cash flow (don't pay early)
- ✅ No overpayment

**Cons:**
- ❌ Complex (need Form 2210 Schedule AI)
- ❌ Must track income quarterly

## State Estimated Tax Payments

### California: Required Separately

California requires **separate estimated payments** if you owe $500+ at tax time.

**Use Form 540-ES** (Estimated Tax for Individuals)

Due dates: **Same as federal** (April 15, June 16, Sept 15, Jan 15)

**Safe harbor:**
- Pay **90%** of current year tax, OR
- Pay **100%** of prior year tax (110% if prior year AGI > $150,000 or $75,000 if married filing separately)

**Example:**
```
2025 CA tax: $25,000
2026 CA expected: $50,000
2026 CA withholding: $30,000

Safe harbor: 100% × $25,000 = $25,000
Withholding: $30,000 > $25,000 ✅

No estimated payments needed
```

### New York: Required Separately

New York requires estimated payments if you owe $300+ at tax time.

**Use Form IT-2105** (Estimated Tax for Individuals)

Due dates: **Same as federal**

**Safe harbor:** Same as federal (90% current or 100-110% prior)

### No-Income-Tax States

If you work in Washington, Texas, Florida, Nevada, Alaska, Wyoming, South Dakota, or Tennessee:

**No state estimated payments required** (no state income tax)

You only pay federal estimated taxes.

---

## How to Make Payments

### Federal Payments

**Option 1: IRS Direct Pay (Free)**

Website: [irs.gov/payments](https://www.irs.gov/payments)

- Link bank account
- Select "Estimated Tax" and tax year
- Choose quarter (Q1/Q2/Q3/Q4)
- Enter amount

**No fees. Instant confirmation.**

**Option 2: EFTPS (Electronic Federal Tax Payment System)**

Website: [eftps.gov](https://www.eftps.gov)

- Enroll (takes 7-10 days for PIN)
- Schedule payments in advance
- View payment history

**Best for recurring payments.**

**Option 3: Credit Card (3% fee)**

Accepted processors: PayUSAtax, Pay1040, ACI Payments

**Fee:** ~2-3% of payment amount

**Only worth it if you get >3% credit card rewards** (rare).

**Option 4: Mail Check**

Use **Form 1040-ES payment voucher**

Mail to IRS address (varies by state)

**Postmark = payment date**

**Slowest option. Use Direct Pay instead.**

### State Payments

**California:**
- Website: [ftb.ca.gov/pay](https://www.ftb.ca.gov/pay)
- Use "Web Pay" (free, instant)
- Or mail Form 540-ES voucher

**New York:**
- Website: [tax.ny.gov/pay](https://www.tax.ny.gov/pay)
- Use "Pay Online" (free)
- Or mail Form IT-2105 voucher

**Other states:** Check your state's Department of Revenue website

## Form 1040-ES: Estimated Tax Worksheet

### How to Fill It Out

**Line 1:** Expected AGI (salary + RSU + stock options + other income)

**Line 2:** Expected deductions (standard deduction or itemized)

**Line 3:** Taxable income (Line 1 - Line 2)

**Line 4:** Tax on Line 3 (use tax tables)

**Line 5:** Other taxes (AMT, self-employment tax, etc.)

**Line 6:** Total tax (Line 4 + Line 5)

**Line 7:** Credits (Child Tax Credit, Foreign Tax Credit, etc.)

**Line 8:** Total tax after credits (Line 6 - Line 7)

**Line 9:** Expected withholding (W-2, RSU withholding)

**Line 10:** Estimated tax to pay (Line 8 - Line 9)

**Line 11:** Prior year tax (from 2025 return Line 24)

**Line 12:** Safe harbor amount (smaller of 90% Line 10 or 100-110% Line 11)

**Line 13:** Required annual payment (Line 12)

**Line 14:** Subtract withholding (Line 13 - Line 9)

**Line 15:** Quarterly payment amount (Line 14 ÷ 4)

## Real Case Study: Shopify TN Worker

**Profile:**
- Salary: $140,000 (Shopify Toronto, remote to US)
- RSU vesting 2026: $200,000 (August)
- State: Washington (no state income tax)
- 2025 tax: $28,000

### Calculation

**Expected 2026 tax:**
```
Gross income: $140K + $200K = $340,000
Standard deduction: -$14,600
Taxable: $325,400

Federal tax: $87,442
```

**Expected withholding:**
```
Salary: $140K × 22% = $30,800
RSU: $200K × 22% = $44,000
Total: $74,800
```

**Shortfall:** $87,442 - $74,800 = **$12,642**

**Safe harbor check:**
```
100% of 2025 tax: $28,000
Withholding: $74,800 > $28,000 ✅

Result: Safe harbor met, no estimated payments needed
```

At tax time, they'll owe $12,642, but **no penalty** (protected by safe harbor).

### Alternative: Increase W-4 Withholding

Instead of owing $12,642 in April, increase withholding:

```
Shortfall: $12,642
Paychecks remaining: 20 (if done in January)

Extra withholding: $12,642 / 20 = $632 per paycheck

File W-4:
Line 4(c): $632
```

Their take-home pay drops by $632/paycheck, but they owe **$0** at tax time.

## Common Mistakes

### ❌ Mistake 1: Not Making Any Estimated Payments

You owe $50,000 at tax time. You didn't make quarterly payments. You didn't meet safe harbor.

**Penalty:** $4,000 (8% × $50,000)

### ❌ Mistake 2: Missing Q1 Payment

You made Q2/Q3/Q4 payments but missed Q1.

**Penalty:** Still applies to Q1 shortfall, even if you caught up later.

### ❌ Mistake 3: Using Last Year's Amount (When Wrong Safe Harbor)

You paid 100% of prior year tax ($30,000), but your prior year AGI was $200,000.

**Correct safe harbor:** 110% × $30,000 = $33,000

You underpaid by $3,000 → **penalty applies**.

### ❌ Mistake 4: Forgetting State Estimated Payments

You paid federal estimated taxes but forgot California.

**California penalty:** 8% on state underpayment (separate from federal)

### ❌ Mistake 5: Not Using Annualized Method

You have big Q4 income but paid evenly in Q1-Q4.

**Result:** You overpaid in Q1-Q3 (gave IRS a free loan), then underpaid in Q4.

**Better:** Use annualized method to match payments to income.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I pay all at once instead of quarterly?

Yes, but you'll still owe penalties for not paying quarterly (unless you meet safe harbor).

The IRS wants **even payments throughout the year**.

### What if I miss a quarterly deadline?

Pay ASAP. Penalty accrues from the due date, but you can minimize it by paying quickly.

### Can I use a credit card?

Yes, but processors charge **2-3% fees**. Only worth it if you get >3% rewards.

### Do I file Form 1040-ES?

No. Form 1040-ES is a **worksheet** + payment vouchers. You use it to calculate payments, but you don't file it with IRS.

You just make the payments (online or by mail).

### What if my income changes mid-year?

Recalculate quarterly payments based on new income. You can adjust future quarters.

Or use annualized income method (Form 2210 Schedule AI).

### Can I get a refund if I overpay?

Yes. Overpayments are refunded when you file your tax return.

But you gave the IRS a **0% interest loan**—better to pay the right amount.

✅ **Use annualized method** (if income is lumpy)  
✅ **Include state payments** (CA, NY, etc.)
